title: Ecuador July 2025 public worker dismissals
point: Quito, seat of the national government and its ministries (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Ecuador has had a 48-month Extended Fund Facility since May 2024. In July 2025 the IMF raised it from US$4 billion to US$5 billion. The program's fiscal plan counts on cutting the public wage bill by 1.2% of GDP over 2024-2028 (IMF Country Report 25/199). No published IMF condition names dismissals or ministry mergers.

conditions: IMF Country Report 25/199 (July 2025, second review) lists wages and salaries as the largest spending item in the program's fiscal adjustment: 0.2% of GDP a year in 2024-2026 and 0.3% in 2027-2028, 1.2% of GDP in total. The report shows no structural benchmark or performance criterion on public jobs. In the government's own policy memorandum to the IMF (Country Report 25/341, December 2025), under the heading Public Sector Wage Bill, the authorities write that 'in June 2025, we streamlined ministries and other public agencies' and plan to keep limiting increases in headcount and wages.
community: On 24 July 2025 government spokesperson Carolina Jaramillo announced that 5,000 public servants in administrative posts in ministries and the social security institute (IESS) would be dismissed; security forces, health staff and teachers were excluded. Local press reported notices arriving from 25 July (Bloomberg Línea). The executive went from 20 to 14 ministries: Culture and Heritage, Sports and Higher Education were merged into Education; Environment into Energy; Women and Human Rights into Government (Peoples Dispatch). Prensa Latina reports a 41% cut in ministries and secretariats. Ecuador had 490,496 public servants (Labour Minister Ivonne Núñez, via Bloomberg Línea). Jaime Carrera of the Observatorio de Política Fiscal estimated savings of under US$50 million a year (Bloomberg Línea). Economist Pablo Dávalos estimated that the IMF-agreed wage cuts would mean about 70,000 public job losses by 2028 (Peoples Dispatch).
outcome: On 25 July 2025 feminist, artistic and cultural groups marched in Quito. The FUT union federation and the teachers' union UNE asked the Constitutional Court to review the decision; citizens, university teachers' unions, judges and prosecutors also brought challenges, and six unconstitutionality suits were filed against the Public Integrity Law (Peoples Dispatch). In December 2025 the government told the IMF the June 2025 streamlining was part of its wage bill effort (IMF Country Report 25/341).

FUT leader Edwin Bedoya said the newly received funds would be used to dismiss public workers, and opposition legislator Virgilio Hernández called the dismissals part of IMF commitments (Prensa Latina). The IMF documents set an overall wage bill cut (1.2% of GDP by 2028) but name no dismissals; the government's December 2025 memorandum to the IMF lists the June 2025 ministry streamlining under wage bill containment. title: Mongolia 2017 IMF program: pay freeze, retirement age and child money cut
point: Sukhbaatar Square, site of the January 2018 union rally

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Three-year Extended Fund Facility agreed February 2017 and approved 24 May 2017. Prior action: passing the 2017 supplementary budget with the fiscal measures needed for program targets (IMF Country Report 17/140).

conditions: IMF Country Report 17/140 (May 2017) lists the program's fiscal measures (savings over 2017-2019): containing the public wage bill (1.4% of GDP), streamlining and better targeting social transfers and reforming public pensions (1.5% of GDP), raising social security contributions (0.6% of GDP), partly reversing a cut in petroleum excise (0.8% of GDP), and a progressive income tax (0.2% of GDP); it also plans to target the Child Money Program to the poorest households. IMF Country Report 17/396 (December 2017) says the 2018 budget adds another year of the public wage and hiring freeze, raises the retirement age (to 65 for men by 2027 and for women by 2037, from 60 and 55), raises the social contribution rate, and limits Child Money to the poorest 60% of children; that targeting was a structural benchmark due end-December 2017.
community: Civil servants' nominal pay was frozen; the IMF notes protests, mainly by doctors and teachers (Country Report 17/396). Child Money was limited to the poorest 60% of children (Country Report 17/396). The UB Post reports that a study found the higher personal income tax hit 11.7% of the population, against 8% expected, and that 1,461 people petitioned parliament's petitions committee against it. Teachers had sought pay rises since August 2017 without result (UB Post); CIVICUS notes a teachers' strike over the pay freeze in November 2017.
outcome: In April 2017 IMF resident representative Neil Saker told the Confederation of Mongolian Trade Unions that Mongolia had 'no other choice rather than raising retirement age', to be phased in gradually (GoGo Mongolia). On 12 January 2018 more than 10,000 people joined a peaceful CMTU rally in Sukhbaatar Square against the retirement age rise and seven tax increases (UB Post; CIVICUS Monitor); the union said it would hold rallies in every province and that members were ready to strike.

title: Nicaragua public pay freeze and job cuts under ESAF

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: ESAF 1994-97 and ESAF/PRGF 1998-2002. In a later program, after a 2005 standoff, the IMF made a real-terms freeze of the overall government payroll a performance criterion (Acevedo, Envío 2008).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Co-prepared the 1994-97 Policy Framework Paper that set the job cut targets.

conditions: Policy Framework Paper 1994-97: cut public employees by 13,500 (about 13%) by end-1996 (7,000 by end-1994, 11,000 by end-1995), described as voluntary; cut about 600 more military posts; freeze public wages and salaries except for a small group; cost recovery measures at the secondary and tertiary levels of education. Acevedo lists secondary school fees as a 1994-97 ESAF performance criterion. The 1998-2002 ESAF required cutting state employment by a further 15,500 (Acevedo, Envío 2008). In 1997 the IMF proposed 10,000 public layoffs and rejected the government's offer of 3,000 (Envío, Sept 1997).
community: Average public worker pay fell from US$140 to US$93 a month between 1992 and 1997, from 74% to 54% of the national average (Treasury Ministry Public Function Division, via Acevedo); total government salary spending fell from about US$157 million to US$105 million (Acevedo). Teachers' take-home pay was about half the national average (Acevedo). Electricity, water and phone rates were raised, as the IMF wanted (Envío, Sept 1997).
outcome: With the signing of ESAF II in 1998 the government accepted about 3,000 more public job cuts, with thousands more expected from privatizations (Envío, Feb 1998). Acevedo (2008) argues the five IMF agreements over sixteen years pushed rural marginalization and poverty to the extreme.

title: Honduras 1990 adjustment package (Callejas)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The Bank waived and released the frozen second tranche of SAL I in June 1990, citing the package (including public job cuts and tariff cuts) as meeting and exceeding its conditions; SAL II followed (World Bank Performance Audit Report, 1996).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Sent a mission in February 1990 alongside the World Bank and IDB; Honduras signed its first IMF stand-by in over a decade in July 1990 (World Bank Performance Audit Report).

conditions: World Bank Performance Audit Report on SAL I, SAL II and the SAC (1996): after parallel Bank, IMF and IDB missions in February 1990, the government announced a 50% devaluation, a revenue rise of 5% of GDP through large public utility tariff increases and taxes, dismissal of 6,000 public employees, import tariff cuts from 90% to 40%, higher interest rate ceilings, and the end of most price controls. The Bank's June 1990 waiver request said these measures 'fundamentally complied with, and in many cases exceeded' SAL I second-tranche conditions.
community: 6,000 public employees dismissed. Consumer prices rose 23.3% in 1990 and 34% in 1991. The real national wage index fell from 100 (1989) to 87.6 (1991). The World Bank notes a significant rise in poverty in 1990, and real per capita income fell slightly over 1990-95 (World Bank Performance Audit Report).
killed_note: No deaths recorded in the sources used.
outcome: The Bank's evaluators judged that the measures laid the groundwork for recovery, but found unemployment, underemployment and poverty stayed around 30% of the labour force through 1990-95 and that Honduras missed major IMF stand-by targets in September and December 1990.

sources.title: Honduras: First and Second Structural Adjustment Loans and Structural Adjustment Credit, Performance Audit Report

confidence_note: The link rests on the World Bank's own evaluation, which treats the package as fulfilling its loan conditions. The only source is the Bank itself; no independent count of the 6,000 dismissals or of protests was found.
check_note: Removed an unsupported reference to Bank poverty assessment data and added the December 1990 missed IMF target. Other figures match the audit report.

title: Honduras Agricultural Modernization Law and reform land sales
point: Lower Aguán Valley near Tocoa, on the north coast, where over 80% of reform-sector land sales took place by 1994 (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Agricultural Sector Adjustment Credit (AGSAC), US$60 million, July 1993. Enacting Law 31-92 with satisfactory land tenure changes was an action required before the credit went to the Board; tranche releases depended on a Land Tenure Action Plan and on divesting the farm bank BANADESA. A BANADESA restructuring plan was agreed under SAL II (1990).

lenders.name: USAID
lenders.role: Merlet (2002) says the law was defined with the help of international advisers, mainly USAID.

conditions: World Bank President's Report P-5923-HO (1993), para. 102: before Board presentation, Law 31-92 (Agricultural Modernization Law, April 1992) with 'satisfactory modifications to the land tenure and forestry policies' had to be enacted and its regulations approved. The law legalised land rental and ended the ban on titling farms under 5 hectares (World Bank); it let reform beneficiaries take individual plots and sell legalised land, and dropped tenancy as grounds for agrarian reform claims (Merlet). Second and third tranches required a plan to divest BANADESA, the main source of formal credit for small farmers, and capping its central bank funding at the August 1991 level, adjusted for inflation. Under SAL II, guaranteed grain prices were replaced by a price band and most state-owned silos were privatized (World Bank).
community: By May 1994 reform-sector farmer groups had sold more than 30,000 ha, just over 7% of reformed land, over 80% of it on the north coast (Merlet, 2002). Within a few years of the law, three large landowners held three-quarters of arable land in the Lower Aguán; some cooperative directors sold common land without members' support (Holland, Carnegie Council, 2014). BANADESA laid off 45% of its staff under the SAL II plan (World Bank, 1993); the Bank's later audit says one-third.
suppression: Holland (2014) reports landowners used 'trickery, threats, harassment, and violence' to press cooperative members to sell. The later Aguán killings (from 2009) are mapped as a separate case.
killed_note: No deaths counted for 1992-1994 in the sources used; the 92 killings in the Lower Aguán cited by Holland from Human Rights Watch cover roughly 2011-2014 and are mapped with the later conflict.
outcome: Merlet (2002) writes that within a few years the effects of land redistribution were seriously undermined, and that new land struggles with violence and repression were emerging, especially in the north. Promised settlement aid and land funds were not put in place. Holland (2014) cites Human Rights Watch's count of 92 killings in the Lower Aguán over three years.
